SEC16A-01.note: Either/or: verb agrees with the nearer subject 'nestmates' (plural), and 'Ever since' plus the ongoing study and present 'is eaten' require present perfect. 'has hauled' is attractive because 'a lone scout' is read first; 'were hauling' gets number right but breaks the 'ever since' tense.

SEC16A-02.note: Fronted 'Only in...' forces inversion; the auxiliary agrees with the delayed singular subject 'assumption' and pairs with 'begun', and 'in the decades since' (to now) needs present perfect: has. 'have' is attracted by 'decades'/'submersibles'/'vents'; 'had' is weakly arguable but lacks a past reference point; 'did ... begun' is never grammatical once 'begun' is found (it lies beyond the four-word window).

SEC16A-03.note: Relative 'that' takes the plural antecedent 'shoots', and shoots are preserved (no object follows), so passive plural: have been preserved. 'has been preserved' is the strong trap, agreeing with 'revival' (the main-clause subject) or 'moss'; full 2x2 number x voice grid.

SEC16A-04.note: Expletive 'there' with a delayed compound subject 'both a strip ... and a fragment' takes a plural verb; the past narrative ('lifted', 'expected') needs past, not present perfect. 'was still concealed' is attractive because 'glue' and 'a strip' are the nearest nouns; 'have long been' gets number right but breaks tense.

SEC16A-05.note: Inverted past counterfactual 'Had one researcher not taken' requires 'would have + participle' in the result clause, and 'then' keeps the result in the past. 'would be dismissed' (mixed conditional) is the most attractive; 'had been dismissed' copies the if-clause form.

SEC16A-06.note: Third member of a series parallel to 'drifted' and 'lingered': headed. 'had headed' is the only real pull (echoing 'had begun' later), but the sequence puts the departure last; 'head' (present) is visibly off-tense.
SEC16A-06.drop_reason: Too easy for the module-2 hard route: the parallel series is settled by 'drifted ... lingered ... and', and the distractors are weak (graded easy cold).

SEC16A-07.note: Series items already containing commas ('starters, some of them...'; 'kefir grains, a dairy culture...'; 'cakes, which...') must be separated by semicolons. All-comma A is the strong distractor (ambiguous list); the double colon in B and the fused 'generations kefir' in C are rejectable on sight.

SEC16A-08.note: The engraver made more than a dozen plates, so the title is restrictive and takes no comma before it. C is the strong trap: the printed comma after the title looks like the closing half of a pair. Weakness: in the key, that comma then sits unpaired before 'because' (acceptable but unusual for an SAT key), so the shared trailing comma actively pushes solvers toward C; D (dash then comma) mismatches.

SEC16B-01.note: Singular head 'mortar' (the 'including...' phrase and the 'a team has argued' interrupter are skipped), and the object 'the hairline cracks' after the interrupter requires active voice: repeatedly seals. 'repeatedly seal' is attracted by 'lumps/fragments'; the passive options fail once the object is found.

SEC16B-02.note: A fraction takes its number from the of-noun: 'two-thirds of the buried carbon' (mass) is singular, and the carbon is carried in by tides, so passive: was actually brought. 'were actually brought' is the strong trap (plural-sounding 'two-thirds'); the active options leave 'brought' with no object.

SEC16B-03.note: When 'each' follows a plural subject ('The two notebooks ... each'), the verb agrees with the plural subject; notebooks are digitized by the volunteers, so passive: are now being digitized. 'is now being digitized' is the strong trap for anyone applying 'each = singular'; full 2x2 number x voice grid.

SEC16B-04.note: After 'carves a new route to the sea,' a result modifier is needed: the present participle 'leaving'. 'left' and 'had left' create a comma-joined second predicate in the wrong tense; 'having left' wrongly puts the stranding before the carving.

SEC16B-05.note: Past-tense reporting verb 'assured' backshifts a future prediction to 'would'; the non-backshifted 'will' is ruled out because 'The opposite occurred' shows the prediction is not still true. 'will keep out' is the main pull; 'had kept out' puts the wall's effect before it existed.

SEC16B-06.note: An age is determined by someone, and nothing follows as an object, so passive; the general-truth framing needs 'can': can be determined. 'can determine' is the only meaningful pull; the 'has/had been' options break the present generic tense.
SEC16B-06.drop_reason: Too easy for the module-2 hard route: a passive voice item with no attractor in number, and the distractors are weak (graded easy cold).

SEC16B-07.note: A complete clause introduces a noun phrase that specifies 'a feature', so a colon. The semicolon is attractive because 'that give' looks like a verb, but 'deep notches ... that give ...' is a noun phrase, not an independent clause; a comma would misattach the phrase to 'magnification'; no punctuation is rejectable on sight.

SEC16B-08.note: A fronted verbless series summed up by 'any one of these' takes a dash. The period in A is the strong trap: it looks clean, but it leaves 'Cold water, acid released by the moss, and ... oxygen.' as a fragment (unless 'released' is misread as a main verb). The comma in B is a splice-like join, and no punctuation is rejectable on sight.

tells: Past perfect never wins: a 'had + participle' option appears in A-01, A-02, A-05, A-06, B-02, B-04, B-05 and B-06 (8 of 12 verb items) and is the key in none. 'Always reject the had-option' strikes a distractor for free in 8 items.
'would' wins both times it is offered with 'will' (A-05, B-05); a 'will' option never wins (A-05, B-05).
Voice: whenever the option set mixes active and passive, the key is the passive in 4 of 5 (A-03, B-02, B-03, B-06); B-01 is the only active key. A 'pick the passive' heuristic scores well.
Full number x voice 2x2 grids (A-03, B-01, B-03) carry no positional or shape tell on their own.
Key letters are balanced (A4 B4 C4 D4); no punctuation mark is always or never the key across A-07, A-08, B-07, B-08, though the semicolon wins only where list items contain commas.

A-08: every option ends in a comma after the title, so the key leaves an unpaired comma; this pushes solvers to the comma-pair distractor C rather than leaking the key, but it is a formatting oddity worth a look.
summary.near_duplicate_notes: A-03/B-03/B-01: number x voice 2x2 grids with a misleading singular attractor (relative 'that' / 'each' / long 'including' modifier). B-02/B-06: passive required because no object follows. A-05/B-05: both keyed 'would...' (counterfactual / backshift). A-01/A-04: correlative and compound-subject agreement. A-02/A-04: delayed subject after an inversion or 'there'.

phase2_note: All 16 keys agree with my cold answers (0 cold misses) and are correct; every explanation's reasoning produces the key and rejects each distractor on a correct rule. A-08's explanation has to excuse the unpaired comma after the title ('simply precedes the because clause'); that is defensible, but the shared trailing comma remains a pull toward C. I recommend dropping only A-06 and B-06, and only because they are too easy for the hard route, not because of any defect. Batch-level tells from phase 1 still stand and the keys confirm them: the past-perfect option loses all 8 times it appears, 'would' beats 'will' in both items that offer the pair, and the passive is the key in 4 of the 5 voice-mixed sets.
